UsersController#create calls user.valid? and later user.save, so the email validator runs twice and do_nothing records are counted twice. The read-modify-write is also not atomic, so concurrent requests can lose increments, and save failures are ignored. Consequence: inaccurate statistics and unnecessary writes."

findings.title: Blocked email lookup is not normalized
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? queries the raw email value without stripping or downcasing it, and BlockedEmail records are not normalized before save. A block for bad@example.com can be bypassed with Bad@Example.com or surrounding whitespace, and the uniqueness validation allows case-variant duplicates. Consequence: blocked email addresses can still be used.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored and under-escaped
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds a case-insensitive regular expression from the setting after escaping only dots and without anchoring the domain. A whitelist entry of example.com will accept user@example.com.evil.com because the address contains @example.com. Other regex metacharacters in the setting are not escaped. Consequence: domain restrictions can be bypassed or misapplied.

findings.title: Side-effecting, non-atomic increment inside validation double counts matches
findings.body: should_block? increments match_count and saves a BlockedEmail record during validation. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and later user.save, so the email validator runs twice and do_nothing records are counted twice. The read-modify-write is also not atomic, so concurrent requests can lose increments, and save failures are ignored. Consequence: inaccurate statistics and unnecessary writes.

findings.title: blocked_emails.email may be shorter than users.email
findings.body: The migration creates blocked_emails.email as a default Rails string, typically varchar(255), while users.email is shown as string(256) in the schema. If a 256-character email is accepted by User, it cannot be stored in blocked_emails, causing insertion failures or inability to block that address.

findings.title: Client-side rejected email list is case-sensitive and not normalized
findings.body: The client-side rejectedEmails check uses exact string equality without normalization. If the server rejects a normalized/lowercased email or the user changes capitalization/whitespace, the UI will not disable submission for that email. This is primarily a UX issue because the server still validates, but it undermines the intended immediate rejection.

findings.title: Missing coverage for normalization and repeated validation passes
findings.body: The specs only test exact-match, single-call behavior for should_block?. They do not cover mixed-case or whitespace variants, nor the fact that User creation can invoke the validator more than once via valid? followed by save. As a result, the blocked-email bypass and double-counting behavior are not caught by tests.
